idiom_name: pthread monitor thread on a pthread_cond_timedwait deadline (CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
implementation_notes: POSIX supplies only the timing primitives - clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC), pthread_cond_timedwait on an absolute deadline, or timer_create with SIGEV_THREAD - so the watchman survives verbatim in C: the arrival path stamps last_seen under a mutex and signals the condition variable, one monitor thread waits for the deadline last_seen + period, and ETIMEDOUT is the absence alarm. The classic structure is not replaced by anything; only its clock and its wake-up are library calls. The timer_create variant can drive a single process-wide watchman without a monitor thread, but then the alert path runs in a signal handler and must stay async-signal-safe.
pitfalls: pthread_cond_timedwait's absolute deadline defaults to the CLOCK_REALTIME origin, so an NTP step or a manual clock change can fire the alarm early or postpone it indefinitely; create the condition variable with pthread_condattr_setclock(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) and keep every timestamp in that clock.

The signal-handler form (alarm/timer_create with SIGEV_SIGNAL) may only call async-signal-safe functions and may only touch volatile sig_atomic_t state; logging, malloc or locking inside the handler is undefined behaviour - hand the event to a thread instead.

Reading the clock with time(NULL) or gettimeofday() makes the watchman wall-clock dependent: after a backwards step last_seen lies in the future and the alarm can never fire - always stamp with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC).
ETIMEDOUT must not be conflated with EINTR or EINVAL from pthread_cond_timedwait; treating any non-zero return as silence alarms on every signal delivered to the process.
The predicate must be re-checked after every wake-up: pthread_cond_timedwait may return spuriously and another thread may have stamped a fresher last_seen.

A producer that signals on every message keeps the monitor thread runnable without ever making the deadline pass, so correctness rests on the re-checked predicate, not on the wake-up count; keep the arrival critical section to a timestamp update so it cannot delay evaluation.

variants.name: POSIX per-process timer with SIGEV_THREAD notification
variants.idiom_name: timer_create(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, SIGEV_THREAD) re-armed on every arrival
variants.implementation_notes: For a single-process watchman without a dedicated thread, arm one timer_create timer per subject and re-arm it (timer_settime with an absolute value) on every arrival; SIGEV_THREAD invokes the notification as a fresh thread, which keeps the alert logic out of signal context at the price of a thread per expiry. The last-arrival bookkeeping is still needed for reporting, but detection is entirely in the kernel timer.
pitfalls: SIGEV_THREAD starts a new thread for every expiry: under repeat-while-silent behaviour that is one thread per alert interval unless the handler re-arms or a state machine suppresses it.
timer_settime with a zero interval is one-shot; a real repeating timer must set it_interval, and mixing both forms in one subject produces either one alert or an unstoppable stream.
